Walk-Forward Analysis, or walk-forward optimization,
is considered by many to be the gold standard in strategy backtesting. It often provides a realistic estimation of
your strategy’s live performance. So what does Walk-Forward Analysis entail? What test settings and performance metrics
should you look out for? I will explain all of that, and perform an
actual analysis on a trend following strategy. Walk forward optimization is a clever extension
of traditional out-of-sample testing, which refers to testing your strategy on data not
previously used for development. It is a simple yet effective means to quantify
your strategy’s sensitivity to changing prices, which is a strong predictor of future
performance. Let me illustrate how Walk forward optimization
works. Suppose you apply a walk-forward optimization
to a basic moving average crossover strategy, where you go long when the price closes above
the moving average, and vice versa for shorts. You have 8 years of data at your disposal. After optimizing over the first in-sample
period from 2010–2012, you determine that the optimal moving average period is 50. You then test your 50-period moving average
over the 2013 data. Next, you move forward your optimization window
by one year, and you find that the optimal period is now 35. You then test your 35-period moving average
over the 2014 data. This cycle of in-sample optimizing and out
of sample testing is repeated as you progress through your entire dataset. If you stitch all your out of sample segments
together, you get a complete out of sample backtest. The example I just illustrated uses unanchored
walk forward optimization, also called rolling or floating walk forward optimization, whereby
the start date of each subsequent in-sample period is moved forward by an amount equal
to the length of each out of sample period. There is an alternative, called anchored walk
forward optimization, whereby the start date of each in-sample period is fixed, meaning
your in-sample periods get longer as you progress through the test. Unanchored walk forward optimization allows
for faster adaptation of your strategy to the prevailing conditions. It is thus more suitable for short-term strategies
or if your market has a changing ‘personality’. Most traders prefer using the unanchored version
for this reason, and this is what we will use from here on out. Walk forward optimization allows your strategy
to adapt to prevailing market conditions through periodic reoptimizations. In this illustration, these reoptimizations
occur yearly, using the most recent historical data. Having multiple optimizations also gives you
a glimpse into your strategy’s parameter stability, which I will demonstrate later
on. More importantly, through walk forward optimization,
you can lengthen the period of your out of sample test, without sacrificing in-sample
data used for parameter optimization. In an ideal world, we would have infinite
data to backtest our strategies on. More data means more trades and more market
conditions; both of these greatly improve the reliability of backtests. If you are looking to run an out of sample
test on the same market, the traditional approach is to allocate a portion of your data for
in-sample development, leaving the remainder untouched for out of sample testing. This creates a conundrum: more in-sample data
is desirable because it trains the strategy to adapt to different market conditions, yet
you want to maximize the amount of data available for out of sample robustness testing. If you split your 8 years of data evenly,
you get a 4-year out of sample backtest. Now compare this to the unanchored walk forward
optimization shown previously. The ratio of in sample data to out of sample
data is 3:1 for each optimization run, yet we manage to get a 5-year out of sample backtest. Therefore, by cleverly manipulating the available
data, Walk forward optimization lengthens both the in-sample training period and the
Out of sample robustness testing period. In fact, the total length of your out of sample
tests can be even longer, depending on your Walk forward optimization settings, which
I’ll explain next. There are two key settings when setting up
a walk forward optimization. First is the number of Optimization Runs. This is the number of times each in-sample
optimization, and out of sample testing cycle is done. There are 5 runs in the illustration here. The next is your Out-of-Sample Percentage. For each run, this is the out of sample data
length in comparison to the in-sample length. A 33% Out of sample % is used here. These two settings can completely change the
complexion of your optimization. The Walk forward optimization on top had 10
runs and a 10% out of sample %, giving a complete out of sample backtest starting from 2012. The bottom one had 30 runs and a 40% out of
sample %, giving a longer out of sample test from 2005. There are trade-offs involved when selecting
your settings. You want to have sufficient runs to ensure
your results are not due to chance. But this also means more frequent reoptimizations,
which can be a hassle if you manage a large portfolio. Likewise, a larger out of sample % produces
a longer overall out of sample test. But if it’s too large, you will likely have
too few trades in the optimization period for a reliable estimate of the optimal strategy
parameters. In general, I recommend the following ranges:
Number of runs should be in the 10–30 range, and the out of sample % should be in the 10—40
range. Finally, the choice of WFO settings should
be in alignment with the premise of your strategy. For example, if you are developing a trend
following strategy on the daily timeframe, it makes little sense to reoptimize on a monthly
basis. Before running any test, we have to establish
what to look out for. The Walk-Forward Efficiency is the ratio of
the annualized out of sample profit over the annualized in-sample profit. Annualized values are necessary since the
lengths of your in-sample and out of sample periods will likely be different. An efficiency of 100% means the out of sample
results are as good as the in-sample results. Some performance deterioration should be expected
when applying your strategy to out of sample data. A minimum efficiency of 50% is often used
as a passing criterion. The Percentage of Profitable Runs is a measure
of your strategy’s consistency. 70% is a good benchmark. And lastly, you want a uniform profit distribution,
meaning each optimization run contributes roughly the same amount to your overall profits. If any of your runs has an abnormally large
contribution, it could be due to an unlikely price shock or market event. Depending on the number of runs you have,
30–50% of total profit should be a good upper limit. To illustrate the application of Walk forward
optimization, I’ll grab a trend following strategy built using StrategyQuant’s genetic
algorithm. Here’s its logic:
This strategy looks for a short-term pullback, as measured by the Parabolic SAR. If this pullback occurs, a buy stop is placed
at the previous week’s opening price. Considering how easily satisfied the Parabolic
SAR conditions are, I believe you can remove them with little consequence. This is essentially a weekly breakout trend
following strategy. Trade management is kept to a minimum, with
only a bar-based time stop and an ATR-based stop loss. There are thus only three optimizable parameters. BarsValid is the Number of bars the entry
buy or sell stops will be valid for. ExitAfterBars addresses the holding period
for each trade, And stop loss coefficient is the multiple applied to the ATR-based stop
loss. We’ll proceed to optimize these. Let’s use a Walk forward optimization setting
that is in the middle of the recommended range above, so we’ll use 20 optimization runs,
and a 20% out of sample %. Using historical data from August 2003 to June 2020, this means
reoptimizing the strategy every 246 days using a history of 1218 days. We get the following walk-forward equity curve. The blue curve shows the strategy’s walk
forward performance, while the grey curve indicates the strategy’s performance with
the static parameter set derived from the genetic algorithm. It is evident that this strategy benefits
from the periodic reoptimizations that Walk forward optimization requires. Perhaps this helped the strategy adapt to
market changes over the 17 years. If you stitch together the out of sample portions
of the optimization, you can get a complete Out of sample backtest from 2007 onwards. A 1.7 profit factor and 11.82 Return/Drawdown
from the out of sample backtest is pretty decent. Let’s now have a look at the walk-forward
metrics for the strategy. We have a 78% walk-forward efficiency, also
called net profit stability. 16/20 runs are profitable, and profits are
evenly distributed with the most profitable run contributing only 16% of overall profit. These give us confidence that the strategy
is both robust and consistent. Let’s now evaluate the strategy’s robustness
from another perspective — using its parameter stability. Here are the resulting parameter sets of the
five most recent optimization runs: Notice that the optimal parameter sets scarcely
change across the years, showing the strategy’s robustness in the face of changing markets. If your strategy does not perform well using
walk-forward optimization, it does not necessarily indicate a lack of robustness. Not all strategies benefit from periodic reoptimizations;
sometimes a static parameter set may work better. If your strategy shows strong long-term performance
with static parameters, don’t hesitate to trade it. Walk-forward optimization can be used to evaluate
your strategy’s robustness, and to determine whether it would benefit from periodic reoptimizations. The process involves breaking down your data
into numerous segments, each containing an in-sample and out-of-sample portion. For each segment, strategy optimizations are
conducted over the in-sample portion, after which the optimal parameters are applied to
the Out of sample portion. Two important settings are the number of runs,
and the percentage of each data segment that will be used for out of sample testing. Be sure to select settings that are aligned
with the premise of your strategy. A robust strategy should consistently demonstrate
strong out of sample performance across the data segments, and ideally across a broad
range of walk forward settings as well. If you want to run walk-forward optimizations
